body.heading: The street is a small community
paragraphs: Most of us live among people we wave at but could not name. Neighbour kindness starts smaller than friendship: a name learned, a wave that becomes a sentence, an eye kept on the house when they are away. Streets where people know each other slightly are measurably pleasanter to live on than streets of strangers.
The first steps are tiny and repeatable. Say hello with the name if you know it. Compliment the garden. Ask which day the bins go out and remember the answer.

body.heading: Offers that are easy to accept
paragraphs: A specific offer is easier to accept than a general one. 'I'm going to the shop — do you need anything?' works where 'let me know if you need anything' politely evaporates. Taking in a parcel, watering plants during a holiday, lending the ladder: small, concrete, done.

Bring the extra portion, not the lecture. Soup when someone is ill, biscuits when a baby arrives, an extra bunch of flowers split between two vases. Food crosses fences that conversation has not yet managed.

body.heading: Kindness without a ledger
paragraphs: The point is not a balance sheet of favours. Some neighbours will give back in kind, some in gratitude, some never — and the street is better anyway. Keep it light, keep it occasional, and let relationships grow at their own pace or not at all.
Children absorb street kindness by osmosis: the neighbour whose name they know becomes a person, and the street becomes a place. That is the quiet curriculum of growing up somewhere friendly.

description: Names learned, parcels taken in, soup when someone is ill: neighbour kindness is built from small, specific, repeatable offers.
